newsitem.title: USA: Asia study shows common disorder goes undiagnosed.
newsitem.headline: Asia study shows common disorder goes undiagnosed.

text.p: A Hong Kong study suggests that people carrying a genetic trait which can cause heart failure may not be getting information on whether it is safe for them to have children, according to a study.
Many people in Hong Kong carrying the blood conditions alpha-thalassemia and beta-thalassemia may not know they have the disorder, according to a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
The two forms of thalassemia are among the world's most common inherited disorders involving a mutation in a single snip of genetic material, known as a gene.

Both affect the red blood cells that carry oxygen to the tissues, making them too fragile. Young adults with the disease, which is common in Mediterranean countries, the Middle East and in Southeast Asia, frequently die of heart failure.

A team led by Dr. Yu-Lung Lau of the University of Hong Kong tested 1,800 students in three high schools and found that five percent carried the defect for alpha-thalassemia and 3.4 percent were carriers of beta-thalassemia.

They used those results to calculate how many babies affected by either form of the disease should be born in Hong Kong, and discovered that the number of women referred for prenatal diagnoses of these disorders is about half of what it should have been.

But the result, said the Lau team, also "demonstrates the feasibility and potential benefits of a community-based screening program" for the two types of thalassemias in Hong Kong and neighbouring provinces in China where the disease is regarded as a significant problem.
